summary: Catalogs a number of known problems found in TCP implementations. It is informational and was written to help implementers spot and fix common mistakes.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2525 is a list of eighteen ways TCP implementations were getting it wrong. Each entry says what the rule is, shows a packet trace of the fault, and explains how to test for it and how to put it right. The bugs matter because a broken sender slows down everyone else on the network, not just its own connection.

subtitle: A catalogue of TCP bugs that break the rules, and how to spot and fix each one

tldr.problem: TCP implementations in the late 1990s broke the rules of TCP in ways that hurt the whole network, not just the connection that hit the bug.
tldr.mechanism: The memo documents eighteen problems, each with a description, the RFC it conflicts with, a packet trace showing the fault, how to detect it and how to fix it. They are grouped into congestion control, reliability, performance and resource management faults.
tldr.outcome: The stated goal is to reduce unnecessary traffic on the network, the rate of connection failures caused by protocol errors, and the load on servers from unsuccessful connections and retransmitted data.

today: RFC 2525 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a catalogue rather than a specification, so the fixes it describes were folded into later implementations and later specifications of TCP rather than into this document.

sections.title: What This Catalogue Is For
sections.content:
The memo catalogues known TCP implementation problems. The goal is to improve conditions in the existing Internet by enhancing the quality of current TCP/IP implementations, and it is hoped that both performance and correctness issues can be resolved by making implementors aware of the problems and their solutions. In the long term, the hope is that this will reduce unnecessary traffic on the network, the rate of connection failures due to protocol errors, and the load on network servers caused by time spent processing unsuccessful connections and retransmitted data, which would help the stability of the global Internet.

Each problem is written the same way. It has a name, which is also the subsection heading. It is classified into one or more of four categories: congestion control, performance, reliability and resource management. There is a description with the background needed to understand it, and a significance section describing the sorts of environment in which the problem matters, followed by implications, the reason the problem is viewed as a problem at all.

The entry then names the RFCs that define the TCP specification the problem conflicts with, using the requirement words MUST, SHOULD and MAY in their usual sense. Where it applies, it gives an ASCII trace file showing the problem and another showing correct behaviour, cites further reading, and explains how to test an implementation to see whether it exhibits the problem, including the difficulties of making the problem appear and of reading traces to detect it. It ends with how to fix the problem, where the cause is known.
sections.plainLanguage: Every entry in the list follows the same shape: what the bug is, why it matters, which rule it breaks, a recording of the traffic that shows it, how to test for it, and how to fix it. That shape is the point. An implementer can pick a bug, reproduce it, and confirm the fix.

sections.title: The Congestion Control Faults
sections.content:
Six problems are about the congestion window, the limit on how much a sender may have in flight. When a TCP begins transmitting, RFC 1122 requires it to start in slow start, with the congestion window initialised to one packet, one segment of the maximum size, and then to increase it by one packet for every acknowledgement received for new data; an experimental change in RFC 2414 allows a slightly larger initial value. A TCP that does not slow start on a new connection sends a burst that stresses the network, causes queueing delay and packet loss, and hurts other connections as well as its own. The trace in the memo shows a host sending six packets totalling 7812 bytes when the agreed maximum segment size of 1460 bytes meant it should have sent at most 1460 bytes at first.

The same fault appears after a retransmission timeout. When a TCP experiences a timeout it must again initialise its congestion window to one packet and increase it by one packet per acknowledgement until it reaches the congestion avoidance threshold, where the congestion avoidance algorithm takes over. The memo calls entering slow start after a timeout one of the cornerstones of Internet congestion stability, and points out that if TCPs fail to do it the network is at risk of congestion collapse. A closely related bug, widely deployed, is the uninitialized congestion window: the slow start mechanism is implemented but the window is never initialised, so the sender bursts. It is fixed by initialising the window on receipt of a SYN ACK, even when the SYN ACK carries no maximum segment size option.

Three further faults change how the window grows or shrinks. Some implementations add an extra fraction of a segment, typically one eighth, when increasing the window in congestion avoidance, which makes the window grow quadratically rather than linearly and can raise the loss rate for everyone sharing a bottleneck. The fix is to remove that term. Some implementations fail to deflate the window properly after loss recovery, so the sender bursts again immediately after recovering and does not reduce its window as much as it should, which may contribute to congestive collapse. And a TCP that retransmits more than one segment after a timeout or a fast retransmit injects more packets into the network than is appropriate; the memo notes that instances of this have been caused by miscomputations involving TCP options, which increase the header beyond its usual size.
sections.plainLanguage: Six bugs are about the limit TCP puts on how much data it may have in flight at once. When the limit is missing, the sender dumps a burst into the network, which queues, loses packets and slows down other people's connections. The rule is simple: start with one segment, add one segment per acknowledgement, and start again from one segment after a timeout.

sections.title: Faults in Retransmission and Loss Recovery
sections.content:
Four problems concern how a sender reacts to loss. Inconsistent retransmission means that for a given sequence number the sender retransmits different data than it sent before, so the receiver may rebuild a different byte stream from the one the sending application produced. Reliable delivery is a fundamental property of TCP, so this fault is critical in every environment. The memo describes one implementation in which the sender received a zero window and stalled, then an acknowledgement arrived offering a larger window, and the sender sent data from beyond the end of its buffer because it used the newly advertised window rather than the length of the data it actually held.

Failure to retain above-sequence data is the second. When a TCP receives a segment whose sequence number is above the next expected one but within the receive window, RFC 1122 says it should queue that segment for later delivery. A TCP that discards it instead causes numerous unnecessary retransmissions during congestion, which aggravates the congestion and can reduce performance by a large factor.

Window probe deadlock is the third. When an application reads a single byte from a full window, the window should not be updated, to avoid Silly Window Syndrome. If the remote peer uses a single byte to probe the window, that byte can be accepted into the buffer, and in some implementations a negative value then arrives in a signed comparison, so all further new data is treated as outside the window and the connection hangs until it times out. The memo traces this to a macro being replaced by a function call for the unsigned maximum: the negative number sign-extends and is treated as the larger value. Changing the call to a signed maximum fixes it.

The fourth is the stretch ACK violation. A receiver may refrain from acknowledging every segment, but acknowledgements should be sent for every second full-sized segment, and if a second full-sized segment does not arrive within a timeout of no more than 0.5 seconds the receiver should send an acknowledgement anyway. A receiver that acknowledges more than two segments at a time makes the sender produce a larger burst for each acknowledgement, which can overwhelm a congested network, and it also slows the growth of the congestion window during slow start.
sections.plainLanguage: Four bugs are about what a sender does when packets go missing. If the sender sends different data the second time, the receiver ends up with a garbled file. If it throws away data that arrived early, it has to ask for it again. If the window arithmetic goes wrong the connection hangs. And if the receiver waits too long to acknowledge, the sender bursts.

sections.title: Timers, Keepalives and Segment Sizing
sections.content:
Five problems are about numbers rather than algorithms. The first is the initial retransmission timeout. When a TCP first begins sending it has no round trip measurements, and RFC 1122 says it should initialise the timeout to 3 seconds. A TCP that uses a lower value experiences very poor performance on long paths, because the timeout expires before the acknowledgement can arrive, so packets are retransmitted needlessly and the connection keeps dropping back into slow start and congestion avoidance. The memo notes that this one should be a one-line change to fix.

The second is failure to back off the retransmission timeout. Each time a segment is retransmitted the timeout should be doubled. If the TCP gives up before waiting long enough, a connection that could have continued is dropped instead. In one implementation the cause was an error in the Brakmo-Peterson round trip time algorithm, which can return a value of zero where the older Jacobson algorithm always returned a positive one; the step that avoided the problem was omitted, so zero was multiplied by the backoff and stayed zero. Backing off the retransmission timer is called a cornerstone of network stability in the presence of congestion, and the RFCs also require the termination of connections after some period of time, at least 100 seconds.

Third and fourth are the keepalive faults. Keepalive is a mechanism for checking whether an idle connection is still alive, and RFC 1122 says it should be used only in server applications that might otherwise hang indefinitely and consume resources if a client crashes or aborts a connection during a network failure. If a keepalive mechanism is implemented it must not interpret a failed keepalive as a failed connection, and the interval between keepalive packets must be configurable and must default to no less than two hours. The first of the two faults is a connection timeout that is too short: if the network is congested or lossy when the probe is sent, and the mechanism does not allow enough time, the connection is dropped even though both peers are still alive. The fix is to time out more slowly, for example by sending nine probes at 75 second intervals and then waiting a further 75 seconds for a response. The second fault is the same problem in the other direction, where the interval between keepalives is too short.

The fifth problem is that TCP options are left out of the maximum segment size calculation. When a TCP works out how much data to put in a packet it calculates a segment size from the path's maximum transmission unit and subtracts the IP and TCP header sizes. If IP options and TCP options are not accounted for, the segment is too large. In implementations using path MTU discovery this can produce packets that are too large for the output interface with the don't fragment bit set, which the local IP layer is not allowed to fragment, so the data cannot be transmitted at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Five bugs are about the numbers a TCP uses. The retransmission timer should start at three seconds and should double every time a segment is resent; too short a timer or no doubling means the connection is torn down while it could still have worked. Keepalive probes should be at least two hours apart and should not be treated as proof that the connection is dead. And the size of a packet has to allow for the options in its headers.

sections.title: Closing and Resetting Connections
sections.content:
Three problems are about how a connection is torn down. When an application closes a connection the TCP should send its FIN promptly, unless the congestion window prevents it. An implementation that waits for unacknowledged data to be acknowledged before sending the FIN exhibits failure to send the FIN notification promptly, and the effect is worst for short-lived connections, where the extra time to close is the greatest relative delay. It also reduces the throughput seen by the application, because connection termination takes longer.

The second problem is failure to send a RST after half duplex close. RFC 1122 says a TCP should send a RST if data is received after a half duplex close, that is, if it cannot be delivered to the application. A TCP that does not can end up with permanently hung connections. The memo says this has been demonstrated when HTTP clients abort connections, which is common when users move to a new page before the current page has finished downloading: the client closes by sending a FIN while the server is still sending images and text, the server's TCP receives the FIN, but its application does not close its side, and the data keeps arriving with nowhere to go. This matters most for endpoints that manage large numbers of connections, because memory and process slots for connection state leak away.

The third is failure to reset on close with data pending. When an application closes a connection so that it can no longer read any received data, the TCP should send a RST if there is unread received data or if new data arrives. A TCP that does not leaves the remote endpoint waiting for the local TCP to act first, which is particularly the case when the local TCP also lets its advertised window fall to zero and does not tear the connection down when the remote side starts probing.
sections.plainLanguage: Three bugs are about hanging up. The closing signal should be sent straight away rather than after waiting for outstanding data. And if data turns up after the connection was closed, the right answer is a reset, which tells the other side to stop. Without it, connections and the memory used to hold them pile up on busy servers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo does not discuss any specific security-related TCP implementation problems, because the working group decided to document those in a separate document. It does note that some of the problems it does discuss can be used for denial-of-service attacks. Those classified as congestion control give an attacker a way to subvert TCPs used for legitimate data transfer into excessively loading network elements. Those classified as performance, reliability and resource management may be exploitable for launching surreptitious denial-of-service attacks against the user of the TCP. Both kinds of attack can be extremely difficult to detect, because in most respects they look identical to legitimate network traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The catalogue says nothing about security bugs in TCP, because a separate document was written for those. What it does say is that several of these faults can be turned into an attack: a sender that ignores the congestion rules can be used to flood the network, and a sender that mishandles timers or resets can be used to hang up other people's connections. Both look like ordinary traffic to a watcher.

WHAT THE FOUR CATEGORIES MEAN FOR AN OPERATOR

items.title: Congestion control
items.text: The sender ignores the limit on data in flight, so the network queues, drops packets and slows down other connections.

items.title: Reliability
items.text: Data is lost, duplicated or the wrong data is resent, so the connection stalls or the wrong bytes arrive.

items.title: Performance
items.text: The connection still works, but it is slower than it should be and uses more of the network than it needs to.

items.title: Resource management
items.text: Connections are never properly torn down, so the memory and process slots used to hold them leak away.
